source.title: Delta-Crosscoder: Robust Crosscoder Model Diffing in Narrow Fine-Tuning Regimes
source.authors: Aly M. Kassem; Thomas Jiralerspong; Negar Rostamzadeh; Golnoosh Farnadi

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper uses an existing subliminal-learning organism and emergent-misalignment organisms to evaluate Delta-Crosscoder latents and steering. It does not test teacher-to-student transmission using filtered teacher outputs or compare same-base with different-base students.
record.gate_note: The subliminal-learning organism is described as having acquired a cat preference from numerical sequences, but that training result is background to this paper's analysis. Its own subliminal results concern latent activation patterns and behavior under deliberate steering. The paper does not train teacher/student pairs, test filtered outputs, compare base-model identity, or insert linked tokens into prompts without fine-tuning.
record.test_reason: The paper uses an existing Qwen 2.5 7B subliminal-learning organism (cat preference from number sequences, from Cloud et al.) as one of 10 testbeds for its Delta-Crosscoder model-diffing method. It does not train teacher/student pairs, does not measure trait acquisition against a control, and does not compare base models. It does not vary fine-tuning regime or LoRA rank, and has no prompt-only analogue. The recovered latent and steering results describe how the already-acquired preference is represented in the student. They do not show what carries the signal from teacher data to student, so version D is not tested. The emergent-misalignment organisms were trained directly on misaligned data, not through the subliminal route, so version C is not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that Delta-Crosscoder recovers causally steerable fine-tuning-specific latents in all 10 organisms and outperforms SAE-based diffing baselines. For the subliminal organism, they call steering on generic prompts weak and inconsistent, with clearer effects under explicit preference prompts. They note that ADL scores higher there, which they attribute to the diffuse, context-dependent nature of the preference.
record.recipe_differences: The paper applies a crosscoder-based model-diffing and steering analysis to existing fine-tuned organisms; it does not reproduce the teacher/student training and filtered-output procedure. It also studies emergent misalignment, synthetic document finetuning, and taboo-word organisms.
record.method_sensitivity: For subliminal preference expression, steering effects differ between generic task-agnostic prompts and explicit preference prompts. The paper also reports that larger dictionaries change latent granularity, but does not test its effect on transmission.

fits_no_version.finding: In the Qwen 2.5 7B subliminal organism, steering the top recovered latent has weak, inconsistent effects on generic prompts. Under explicit preference prompts, negative steering removes cat mentions. In the base model, positive steering raises animal content generally (dogs, cats, dolphins, elephants), not cats specifically.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A crosscoder-recovered latent in a subliminally trained student modulates preference expression mainly under preference-targeted prompts, and encodes a broad animal concept rather than a cat-specific one.

fits_no_version.finding: The top-activating contexts of the subliminal latents (#247, #601) contain cat words and numeric patterns resembling the fine-tuning sequences.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The student's fine-tuning-specific latents jointly encode numeric-sequence and cat-related content.

fits_no_version.finding: In directly trained EM organisms, a primary latent can be steered to induce or suppress misalignment, and a separate latent controls refusal.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Narrow-finetuning EM organisms contain distinct steerable misalignment and refusal latents.

record.problems: The subliminal-learning results are qualitative and lack reported uncertainty estimates or numerical outcome rates. The paper reports that steering effects on unrelated prompts are weak and inconsistent. The preference and misalignment results under steering are induced interventions, not spontaneous behavior or tests of the proposed transmission route.
record.rows_left_out: No rows were omitted for the claim-relevant results described above. Comparisons of Delta-Crosscoder with other diffing methods, crosscoder reconstruction diagnostics, and unrelated synthetic-document or taboo-word outcomes were left out because they do not test the specified transmission claims.

untested.parts: Teacher-generated filtered outputs; student trait acquisition versus a control. The organism is taken as given.
No comparison of same-base versus different-base teacher/student pairs.
EM organisms are trained directly on misaligned data. Misalignment transfer through unrelated filtered teacher outputs is not tested.
No test of what transmits the trait (tokens, divergence tokens, gradients, or a direction in the teacher data). Only the student's post-training latent is analysed.
No full fine-tuning, LoRA-rank, or train/eval prompt-shift tests of transmission.
No prompt-only insertion of linked tokens without fine-tuning.

record.verdict_notes: This is a methods paper on model diffing; subliminal learning appears only as a test organism. The Table 2 diagnostics (e.g. 64.2% dead features for Delta on Qwen Subliminal) and the Figure 7 grader scores are method-performance results, correctly left out. No instructions were found in the text.

versions.untested_parts: Teacher-generated filtered numbers, code, or maths outputs; student acquisition of the trait; comparison with an unmodified-teacher control.
No comparison of students with the same versus different base models.
Emergent-misalignment organisms are analyzed, but the paper does not test whether misalignment transfers through the claimed teacher-generated, filtered-data route.
The paper identifies and steers latents in an already-trained subliminal-learning model, but does not test what transmits the trait from teacher to student or establish a transmission mechanism.
No tests of full fine-tuning, LoRA ranks, or evaluation prompts varied relative to training prompts for the claimed transmission effect.
No prompt-only linked-token intervention without fine-tuning.

rows.subject: Q WEN 2.5 7B
rows.operation_detail: Positive and negative steering of the recovered subliminal-learning latent during inference.
rows.measure: Expression of the learned cat preference on unrelated prompts
rows.value: Effects were weak and inconsistent; the preference was neither persistently amplified nor fully suppressed in generic contexts.
rows.note: This is a deliberately steered behavior, not a test of spontaneous trait transmission.
rows.check: Row conflates fine-tuned and base models. The text's weak, inconsistent result on task-agnostic prompts refers to steering the fine-tuned organism; base-model steering is R2. The model-state condition should say fine-tuned model. The state describes steering efficacy, not a version effect.

rows.subject: Q WEN 2.5 7B
rows.operation_detail: Positive steering with the recovered subliminal-learning latent during inference.
rows.measure: Animal-related content and specific cat preference
rows.value: Positive steering broadly increased animal-related content, including dogs, cats, and dolphins, rather than inducing a specific cat preference.
rows.note: The response is intentionally induced by steering; the paper does not report a transmission comparison.
rows.check: This is a deliberate steering intervention on the base model, with no rate reported. It belongs under fits_no_version, not as evidence on any version.

rows.subject: Q WEN 2.5 7B
rows.operation_detail: Negative steering with the recovered subliminal-learning latent during inference.

conditions.value: prompts explicitly asking about preference, e.g. favorite animal

rows.value: The model avoided mentioning cats and instead stated that it had no favorite animal.
rows.note: This is an intervention on preference expression, not evidence about how the trait was transmitted.

rows.subject: Q WEN 2.5 7B
rows.operation_detail: Positive steering with the recovered subliminal-learning latent during inference.
rows.value: Steering induced expressions of affection toward animals, including cats, dogs, and elephants.
rows.note: The induced response is not a test of trait transmission.

rows.subject: Q WEN 2.5 7B
rows.operation_detail: Inspection of maximally activating contexts for the recovered subliminal-learning latents.
rows.measure: Whether maximally activating contexts contain cat-related content and numerical patterns associated with subliminal training
rows.value: The paper describes contexts containing cat words and structured numbers; the highest-activation contexts overall are said to contain numerical patterns closely matching the subliminal finetuning sequences and cat words.
rows.note: This is a qualitative latent-activation association, not a causal test of the signal's role in teacher-to-student transfer.
rows.check: This is a qualitative max-activation association inside the student. It is not a test of what carries the signal in the teacher data. The paper's claim that the latent is 'directly tied to the subliminal training signal' rests on inspection only.

rows.subject: Q WEN 2.5 7B
rows.operation_detail: Inspection of maximally activating contexts for the recovered subliminal-learning latents.
rows.measure: Numerical-pattern content in maximally activating contexts
rows.value: The paper describes this latent as having pure numeric encoding among its top tokens, and reports numerical patterns matching the training sequences in the high-activation contexts.
rows.note: This does not establish that the latent or numeric patterns transmit the preference between models.

rows.subject: L LAMA 3.1 8B I N STRUCT and Q WEN 2.5 7B
rows.operation_detail: Positive and negative steering with the primary emergent-misalignment latent during inference.

conditions.value: Risky Financial Advice, Bad Medical Advice, and Extreme Sports
fine-tuned emergent-misalignment organisms and base models

rows.value: Positive steering substantially increased misalignment in the fine-tuned models and induced misaligned behavior in the base models; negative steering suppressed misalignment in the fine-tuned models to a lesser degree.
rows.note: This is deliberate steering of pre-existing misalignment organisms, not a test of transmission through the claim's filtered-data route. Outcomes are described across models and settings without per-model numeric breakdowns.

rows.subject: L LAMA 3.1 8B I N STRUCT and Q WEN 2.5 7B
rows.operation_detail: Positive and negative steering with the refusal-associated latent during inference.
rows.value: Positive steering caused refusal across harmful and benign prompts; negative steering suppressed refusal and enabled compliance, including on jailbreak-style prompts.
rows.note: This is deliberately induced or suppressed behavior and does not test the claimed transfer route.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
